blocks.content: When two systems communicate via an API, the data has to travel as bytes. How those bytes are structured the format has a huge impact on speed, size, readability, and compatibility. The three formats you will see most in system design are JSON, Protobuf, and Avro.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274947616-153784327.png
blocks.alt: JSON, Protobuf, and Avro trade readability and size against each other in three different ways

blocks.content: Think of data formats like packing luggage:
JSON → You pack items with clear labels on each one (like "shirt" "shoes"). Anyone can open the bag and understand what's inside without help. It's simple and human-readable, but takes more space.

Protobuf → You pack items very tightly in a small bag with no labels. It saves a lot of space and is fast to move, but the person opening it needs a separate "packing guide" (schema) to understand what's inside.

Avro → Similar to Protobuf (compact and efficient), but you also include the "packing guide" inside the bag itself. So it's still space-efficient, and anyone can unpack it without needing extra information separately.
Same data three very different representations in memory and over the wire.
1. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)
A common data format used in APIs. It’s human-readable and self-describing every piece of data includes its field name, so anyone can understand it without extra instructions.
Key Idea
["Data is stored as key-value pairs","Keys (like \"id\", \"name\") are always included with the data","Easy to read, debug, and use across systems"]
items: Keys (like "id", "name") are always included with the data
Easy to read, debug, and use across systems

blocks.content: Trade-off
["Verbose → field names repeat every time","Takes more space compared to compact formats like Protobuf or Avro"]
items: Takes more space compared to compact formats like Protobuf or Avro

blocks.content: Pros and Cons of JSON
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274949563-416642063.png
blocks.alt: JSON is readable and simple, at the cost of repeating field names and taking more space

blocks.content: 2. Protocol Buffers (Protobuf)
A binary data format by Google designed to be fast, compact, and efficient.
Unlike JSON, it does not send field names, only small field numbers defined in advance.
1. Schema File (.proto)
This is the most important part. You define structure once:
What this means:
["order_id = 1 → field number is 1","customer_id = 2 → field number is 2","These numbers are what actually go over the network"]
items: These numbers are what actually go over the network

blocks.content: Think: field number = shortcut instead of field name
2. Same Data in JSON (for comparison)
Problem:
["\"order_id\", \"customer_id\" repeated every time","Takes more space"]
3. Protobuf Internal Representation (Conceptual)
Instead of sending:
"order_id": "ORD-9921"
It sends:
Instead of:
"customer_id": "USR-441"
It sends:
Field names completely removed
4. Actual Wire Format (Binary)
Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) is just a faster and smaller way to send data between systems.

Instead of sending data in readable text like JSON (which repeats field names and is bulky), Protobuf uses a predefined schema that both sides already know. So when data is sent, it replaces field names with small numbers and converts everything into a compact binary format.
Because of this:
["Data size is much smaller","Processing is faster","Network usage is lower"]
The downside is:
["You can’t read it directly (not human-friendly)","Both sender and receiver must agree on the schema beforehand"]
items: You can’t read it directly (not human-friendly)
Both sender and receiver must agree on the schema beforehand

blocks.content: Both sender and receiver already know the same schema (.proto file), so they don’t need to send field names or extra information with the data.
They just send compact binary data with tiny numeric tags, and the receiver uses the same schema to understand what each number means.
Pros and Cons of Protobuf
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274951086-746852392.png
blocks.alt: Protobuf is small and fast but not human-readable, and both sides need the same schema file

blocks.content: How To Create .proto file File
Step 1: This defines the structure (contract)of data that both sender and receiver agree on.
Step 2: This creates data and converts it into compact binary format to send over network.

# Step 2: Serialize (sender)
from order_pb2 import Order, OrderItem

order = Order(
  order_id="ORD-9921",
  customer_id="USR-441",
  items=[OrderItem(product_id="BOOK-001", name="Clean Code", qty=2, price=499.0)],
  total=998.0,
  status="confirmed"
)

binary_data = order.SerializeToString()

blocks.content: 3. Apache Avro
Binary format like Protobuf, but the schema travels with the data (or is stored in a schema registry). Big in the Hadoop/Kafka ecosystem. Schema is written in JSON, data is compact binary.
Think of Apache Avro like this:

When systems talk to each other, they need to send data. The easiest way is JSON, but JSON is bulky because every message repeats field names like "orderId", "customerId", etc. That makes it slow and heavy at scale.
Avro solves this by sending only the actual values in a compact binary form. It removes all the extra text. But then the question is: how does the receiver know what each value means?
That’s where the schema comes in.
The schema is just a JSON file that says:
["what fields exist","their order","their types"]
Both sender and receiver use this schema. So instead of sending:
{ "orderId": "ORD-1", "total": 100 }
Avro sends something like:
[ORD-1, 100]  → (in binary, not readable)
And the schema tells:
["first value = orderId","second value = total"]
So data becomes small + fast, but still understandable.
Now the most important part: changes over time
In real systems, you will update your data. Maybe tomorrow you add a new field like status.
With Avro, this doesn’t break things.
["Old systems can still read new data","New systems can read old data"]
items: Old systems can still read new data
New systems can read old data

blocks.content: As long as you define defaults properly
That’s called schema evolution, and it’s the main reason Avro is used in real-world systems.
The schema (structure) is always available either inside the data or in a Schema Registry (like in Kafka).
Because of this, data can change safely over time.
If you add a new field with a default value:
["Old systems can still read the data","New systems can use the new field"]
items: Old systems can still read the data
New systems can use the new field

blocks.content: So nothing breaks.
Pros and Cons of Avro

blocks.alt: Avro stays compact while carrying its schema along, trading that off against slower reads

blocks.content: Now we already understand the serialization of data using these three things. Now let's test it.
For that, I will rewind it again for you.

Serialization means taking an object (data in your program) and converting it into a format that you can save (like in a file or database) or send over a network, and later convert it back into the original object.
Common Serialization Formats:

["JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)
A simple text format that is easy for humans to read and write. It’s very popular for APIs and data exchange.","Avro
A compact binary format created by Apache. It is fast and supports changing data structures over time (schema evolution).","Protobuf (Protocol Buffers)
A binary format made by Google. It is very fast and uses less space, making it efficient for communication between systems."]
items:
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)
A simple text format that is easy for humans to read and write. It’s very popular for APIs and data exchange.

Avro
A compact binary format created by Apache. It is fast and supports changing data structures over time (schema evolution).

Protobuf (Protocol Buffers)
A binary format made by Google. It is very fast and uses less space, making it efficient for communication between systems.

blocks.content: Objective of the Tests
The goal was to compare these formats based on:
["Data size after serialization","Speed of serialization and deserialization","Memory usage"]
We also wanted to show how implementation choices can affect performance.
Test Setup
We created a dataset of 1,000,000 Person objects with random data to run the tests.

We checked how each format performs by looking at three things: how big the data becomes after conversion, how long it takes to convert the data to and from that format, and how much memory it uses during the process.
4.1 JSON
JSON Results and Explanation
When using JSON,
The final data size was around 9 MB. It took about 0.92 seconds to convert the data into JSON and 0.34 seconds to convert it back. The memory usage was around 40 MB.
JSON is simple and easy to understand since it is human-readable. However, it takes more space and is slower compared to binary formats, which makes it less efficient for high-performance use cases.
4.2 Protobuf
Schema Definition (person.proto):
Serialization and Deserialization:
Protobuf Results and Explanation
With Protobuf,
The data size was much smaller at around 4.7 MB. It took about 0.50 seconds to serialize and only 0.01 seconds to deserialize. Memory usage was also low, around 4.5 MB.
Protobuf is very fast and efficient, making it great for performance-critical systems. However, it needs a predefined schema and the data is not human-readable, which makes debugging a bit harder.
4.3 Avro with fastavro
Schema Definition:
Serialization and Deserialization:
Avro Results and Explanation
With Avro,
The data size was the smallest at around 4.2 MB. However, it took about 3.40 seconds to serialize and a very high 47.32 seconds to deserialize. Memory usage was also quite high at around 117 MB.

Avro is great for reducing data size and supports flexible schemas. But in this case, it performed poorly in terms of speed and memory, especially during deserialization, making it less suitable for performance-heavy tasks.
5. Final Analysis
Avro gives the smallest data size, then Protobuf, and JSON is the largest. Smaller size is useful when you want to save storage or reduce network usage.
When it comes to speed,
Protobuf is the fastest for both converting data and reading it back.
Avro is much slower, especially while reading the data, which can be a problem if your system needs quick responses.
In terms of memory, Avro uses a lot more memory compared to the others, which can be an issue on systems with limited resources.
6. Why Code Matters
Performance is not just about the format you choose, but also how you write your code. Better implementation can make a big difference.
For example, improving libraries or optimizing logic can speed things up. Reading data in small parts (streaming) instead of loading everything at once helps reduce memory usage and improves speed.
Also, keeping your schema and data structure aligned avoids unnecessary overhead.
7. Conclusion

["If you need speed, go with Protobuf.
","If you care more about smaller data size, Avro can help but needs careful handling.
","If you want simplicity and readability, JSON is still a good choice."]
items: If you need speed, go with Protobuf.
If you care more about smaller data size, Avro can help but needs careful handling.
If you want simplicity and readability, JSON is still a good choice.
